question: How do finite width and depth change the angle between two inputs propagated through a randomly initialized plain ReLU network, and can predicted angle collapse diagnose trainability?

key_findings.claim: For the paper's bias-free Gaussian ReLU MLP, the angle between two post-activation vectors evolves as a width-dependent Markov process.
key_findings.evidence: Conditional Gaussianity, ReLU homogeneity, critical He scaling, and independent layers make the next angle depend on the incoming angle and layer width rather than earlier states.

key_findings.claim: A small-angle large-width approximation adds a finite-width contraction of roughly 2/n per layer to the infinite-width correlation collapse.
key_findings.evidence: Approximation 1 updates log sin-squared angle by a term -2 theta/(3 pi) and a positive rho(n)=2/n+O(n^-2). Iterating the deterministic update suggests exponential typical collapse in cumulative reciprocal width, versus an approximately reciprocal-depth infinite-width angle.

key_findings.claim: Theorem 1 computes one-step large-width mean and variance expansions for the log-sine angle at a fixed incoming angle.
key_findings.evidence: The conditional mean and variance are expressed through Gaussian ReLU mixed moments J_a,b(theta), with O(n^-2) remainder for the stated one-layer limit. The small-angle corollary retains additional theta/n terms and a leading variance near 8/n.

key_findings.claim: The paper develops exact recurrences and a Bessel-number path formula for Gaussian ReLU mixed moments used by the angle expansion.
key_findings.evidence: Gaussian integration by parts gives recurrences for J_a,b, and Theorem 5 solves the two-index recursion with weighted paths whose coefficients are Bessel numbers, supplemented by boundary cases and symmetry.

key_findings.claim: Monte Carlo experiments support the proposed one-step moments and iterated log-Gaussian approximation in the tested width and depth range.
key_findings.evidence: Five thousand width-256 networks propagated an initial angle 0.1 through 30 layers, and 10,000 width-1024 one-step networks covered 100 angles from 0.005 to 0.8. Predicted means and variances track the simulations, with reported KS p-values 0.987 at layer 1 and 0.186 at layer 30.

key_findings.claim: Across 45 hand-designed plain MLP architectures, a more collapsed predicted final angle is associated with worse one-epoch image-classification accuracy.
key_findings.evidence: Architectures of depth 2-50 and varied widths are trained ten times on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 using Adam and Keras defaults; test accuracy is plotted against the predicted log angle for two initially orthogonal inputs.

key_findings.claim: At literal finite width, the unregularized log-sine moments appear mathematically undefined on positive-probability ReLU events.
key_findings.evidence: A next-layer ReLU vector can be exactly zero with positive probability and nonzero pairs can also become collinear, so theta can be undefined or log sin-squared theta equals minus infinity. The theorem does not condition these events away or introduce an epsilon-regularized logarithm.

key_findings.claim: The exponential depth-degeneracy statement and Gaussian transition are heuristics rather than controlled joint depth-width theorems.
key_findings.evidence: The proved expansion is one-step at fixed incoming angle, while repeated collapse drives theta toward the boundary where uniform error constants are not supplied. Approximation 1 drops a leading O(1/n) variance, and no CLT is proved for the dependent pair-sum statistic used in Approximation 2.

key_findings.claim: A single pairwise initialization angle is not yet a validated architecture-selection criterion.
key_findings.evidence: The accuracy study confounds depth, width, parameter count, and a fixed one-epoch budget, provides no trained-to-convergence or held-out ranking test, and does not compare with Gram spectra, Jacobian conditioning, NTK metrics, or established zero-cost NAS scores.

method.core_idea: Retain finite-width fluctuations in the layerwise correlation dynamics of a random ReLU MLP and summarize them through the logarithm of the squared sine between two representations.
method.mechanism: The next layer's norms and inner product are sums of correlated ReLU-Gaussian variables. Mixed moments, a delta-method expansion, and small-angle series yield conditional mean and variance formulas; a Gaussian transition iterates them through depth. The predicted final angle is then compared with brief training performance across architectures.
assumptions: Layers are fully connected, bias-free, independent, standard-Gaussian, and critically He-scaled.
The activation is exact ReLU and there are no residual paths, normalization layers, convolutions, or attention.
Width is large while the incoming angle is fixed for the proved one-step asymptotics.
A Taylor expansion of log around positive empirical moments remains valid despite lower-tail events.
The standardized next log-angle is approximately Gaussian.
The behavior of one input pair at initialization predicts dataset-level training quality.

techniques.role: Reduces representation propagation to a one-dimensional stochastic state conditioned on layer width.
Approximates conditional mean and variance of log sin-squared angle through order 1/n.
Expresses all needed norm and correlation moments as J_a,b(theta).
Computes high-order mixed moments via integration-by-parts recurrences and combinatorial paths.
Simulates depth evolution with a fitted Gaussian conditional transition.
Uses predicted final separation of two orthogonal inputs as a cheap architecture score.

evaluations.setting: 5,000 width-256 random ReLU networks, initial angle 0.1, propagated through 30 layers.
evaluations.metric: Distribution, mean, variance, and KS comparison of log sin-squared angles.
evaluations.result: The iterated approximation visually tracks the empirical distribution through the tested depth; KS tests do not reject at layers 1 or 30.
evaluations.baseline: Direct Monte Carlo simulation of the exact random network.

evaluations.setting: 10,000 width-1,024 one-step networks at each of 100 initial angles from 0.005 to 0.8.
evaluations.metric: Conditional mean and variance with 99% Monte Carlo intervals.
evaluations.result: The analytic one-step formulas agree closely over most of the tested range.
evaluations.baseline: Monte Carlo estimates and the simpler small-angle approximation.

evaluations.setting: 45 dense plain MLP architectures of depth 2-50, each trained ten times for one epoch on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10.
evaluations.metric: Test accuracy versus predicted final log-angle from an orthogonal input pair.
evaluations.result: Severe predicted angle collapse is associated with low brief-training accuracy, including CIFAR-10 values only around 0.14-0.37.
evaluations.baseline: Other hand-designed architectures in the same sweep; no established NAS-score baseline.

limitations: The finite-width log observable has positive-probability singular events unless the theorem is conditioned, truncated, or regularized.
The Taylor remainder for log is not uniformly controlled near zero by the central-moment bounds given.
One-step fixed-angle O(n^-2) asymptotics do not control accumulated error when depth grows with width and the angle approaches zero.
The Gaussian approximation is motivated by simulations and CLT intuition but no dependent-statistic CLT is proved.
The architecture excludes the residual connections, normalization, biases, smooth activations, convolutions, and attention that prevent or alter collapse in practical networks.
One pairwise angle cannot capture dataset-wide rank, class geometry, Jacobian conditioning, gradient propagation, or trainability after representation learning.
The architecture study trains for only one epoch under one optimizer, conflates scale axes, and lacks held-out or compute-matched ranking evaluation.
Failure to reject a KS null is described too strongly as statistical indistinguishability.
failure_modes: All neurons for one input can be inactive, making the next normalized representation and its angle undefined.
Collinear activation patterns can set sin-squared angle to zero and the log to minus infinity.
Small per-layer approximation bias can compound over depths comparable to width.
A Gaussian transition assigns support outside the true bounded log-angle domain.
Residual or normalization layers can preserve information even when the plain-MLP score predicts collapse.
Two chosen inputs can remain separated while other dataset directions collapse, or vice versa.
One-epoch accuracy can reward optimization speed rather than final expressivity or generalization.
reusable_insights: Finite-width effects accumulate with cumulative reciprocal width, so depth and width should be scaled jointly rather than analyzed in isolation.
Before taking logs of random geometric quantities, audit atoms at zero and supply truncation or lower-tail bounds.
Keep one-step asymptotics, iterated stochastic approximations, and deterministic typical-scale heuristics explicitly separate.
Architecture diagnostics should aggregate a dataset-level Gram spectrum and compare against gradient/Jacobian/NTK baselines.
Validate initialization metrics both for early optimization and convergence under modern residual and normalized architectures.
open_questions: Can an epsilon-regularized or conditioned log-angle theorem control zero-activation and collinearity events rigorously?
What joint limit holds when depth, width, and inverse angle all grow together?
Can a U-statistic or dependency-aware CLT justify the proposed log-Gaussian transition with boundary control?
How do residual paths, normalization, biases, orthogonal weights, and smooth activations change finite-width angle dynamics?
Does a dataset Gram-spectrum degeneration score outperform established zero-cost NAS proxies on held-out architectures?
Can training dynamics reverse severe initialization collapse, and what optimizer or architecture components enable recovery?

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Information Propagation
competitive_landscape.difference: Deep Information Propagation derives mean-field correlation and gradient depth scales and the edge of chaos; the target's main addition is an explicit finite-width stochastic correction to ReLU angle propagation.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Limits and a Cut-Off Phenomenon for Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Avelin and Karlsson use semi-invariant metrics and ergodic theorems to establish deep limits and cutoff phenomena for broader layer maps; the target gives more explicit ReLU log-angle moment formulas but weaker depth-uniform control.

competitive_landscape.title: The Future is Log-Gaussian: ResNets and Their Infinite-Depth-and-Width Limit at Initialization
competitive_landscape.difference: This work derives log-Gaussian effects when ResNet depth and width grow at fixed ratio and proposes Balanced ResNets; the target studies exact plain ReLU and approximates its finite-width angle transition without residual protection.

competitive_landscape.title: Rapid training of deep neural networks without skip connections or normalization layers using Deep Kernel Shaping
competitive_landscape.difference: Deep Kernel Shaping actively selects nonlinearities and initialization to prevent kernel/correlation pathologies and validates training on modern image tasks; the target characterizes unmodified ReLU collapse and offers a diagnostic rather than a remedy.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Tangent Kernel Beyond the Infinite-Width Limit: Effects of Depth and Initialization
competitive_landscape.difference: The NTK analysis targets finite-width kernel dispersion and training evolution when depth is comparable to width; the target focuses on forward representation angles and then only correlates them with brief training.

competitive_landscape.title: The Neural Covariance SDE: Shaped Infinite Depth-and-Width Networks at Initialization
competitive_landscape.difference: The Neural Covariance SDE derives a joint stochastic covariance limit using depth-dependent activation shaping; the target uses fixed exact ReLU and a discrete approximate log-angle kernel.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Finite width causes exponentially vanishing representation angles in deep plain ReLU networks, and the resulting depth-degeneracy score predicts architecture trainability.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper derives detailed one-step mixed-moment asymptotics, constructs a log-Gaussian transition, validates it by Monte Carlo, and correlates predicted collapse with one-epoch classification accuracy.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The explicit finite-width ReLU moment machinery is substantial and the cumulative reciprocal-width perspective is useful. The strongest theorem and exponential language need repair: literal log moments have zero-event singularities, joint depth-angle error is uncontrolled, and the architecture score is only a confounded early-training correlation.

reviewer_notes: Read all 45 extracted pages and independently audited the proofs, moment recurrences, simulations, and complete architecture appendix. The key proof caveat is structural rather than editorial: finite-width ReLU has positive-probability zero/collinear events incompatible with unconditioned log moments. Six primary theoretical and practical comparators were checked on arXiv and JMLR on 2026-08-23.
